description: Team of passionate problem-solvers combining skills in software development, data analysis, and creative design. We love turning NASA's open data into impactful solutions for space and Earth challenges. We bring experience in coding, rapid prototyping, and teamwork under pressure. We're looking for members skilled in AI/ML, UI/UX design, data visualization, or storytelling and pitching. If you're curious, collaborative, and ready to innovate, join us and let's build something out of this world!
summary:
> Earth Detective is an interactive web app that helps people explore how air temperature has changed over time at a location they choose. Users select a point on a world map or enter coordinates, choose a date range, and visualize monthly temperature data from NASA POWER. The app shows the observations, data coverage, and a descriptive trend, with details about the source and method. Users can also save an analysis and export the data as a CSV.
>
> The project addresses the challenge by turning NASA Earth data into a tool people can use to investigate questions about places they care about. A built-in example from Ceará, Brazil, demonstrates how to interpret a short temperature record and understand the limits of its conclusions.
details:
Earth Detective is an interactive web app for exploring how air temperature has changed at a location. Users can select a point on a world map or enter its coordinates, choose a date range, and run an analysis. The app retrieves monthly air temperature at 2 meters from NASA POWER, plots the observations, and calculates a descriptive trend. Each result includes the selected location, the period analyzed, data coverage, and the source and method. Users can reopen saved analyses and export the monthly values as a CSV.

We built Earth Detective so students, educators, and curious members of the public can investigate places they care about without writing code. The map makes it easy to start with a local question, and the chart keeps the monthly observations visible alongside the fitted trend. Our example from Ceará, Brazil, shows how 48 monthly observations can describe change at one grid cell while illustrating the limits of drawing broader conclusions from a four-year record.

We built the interface with React and TypeScript, using Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the street map and MapLibre GL for the optional 3D globe. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, and Scrapling to retrieve and process NASA POWER data, and SQLite stores saved analyses.

Our team considered global data coverage, seasonal variation, and how to explain what a trend means at a single point. We also considered different devices and graphics capabilities. The app opens in a lightweight 2D map, loads the 3D globe on demand, and offers coordinate entry for users who prefer the keyboard.
